claim: Neuronal ensembles are coactive groups of neurons found in spontaneous and evoked cortical activity.
source: Neuronal ensembles, coactive groups of neurons found in spontaneous and evoked cortical activity, are causally related to memories and perception, but it is still unknown how stable or flexible they are over time.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a definition and background for the study.

claim: Neuronal ensembles are causally related to memories and perception.
source: Neuronal ensembles, coactive groups of neurons found in spontaneous and evoked cortical activity, are causally related to memories and perception, but it is still unknown how stable or flexible they are over time.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Less than half of the neurons remained active across any two imaging sessions.
source: Less than half of the neurons remained active across any two imaging sessions.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1K.

claim: Stable neurons formed ensembles that lasted weeks.
source: These stable neurons formed ensembles that lasted weeks, but some ensembles were also transient and appeared only in one single session.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Some ensembles were transient and appeared only in one single session.
source: These stable neurons formed ensembles that lasted weeks, but some ensembles were also transient and appeared only in one single session.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: Stable ensembles preserved most of their neurons for up to 46 days.
source: Stable ensembles preserved most of their neurons for up to 46 days, our longest imaged period, and these 'core' cells had stronger functional connectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: Core cells in stable ensembles had stronger functional connectivity.
source: Stable ensembles preserved most of their neurons for up to 46 days, our longest imaged period, and these 'core' cells had stronger functional connectivity.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 4H.

claim: The longest imaged period was 46 days.
source: Stable ensembles preserved most of their neurons for up to 46 days, our longest imaged period, and these 'core' cells had stronger functional connectivity.
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the abstract as a methodological detail.

claim: Neuronal ensembles could serve as a substrate for long-lasting representation of perceptual states or memories.
source: Our results demonstrate that neuronal ensembles can last for weeks and could, in principle, serve as a substrate for long-lasting representation of perceptual states or memories.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings, involving speculation about functional implications.

claim: Neuronal ensembles are thought to underlie neural representations of memories, perceptions, thoughts, motor programs, computations, or mental states.
source: Neuronal ensembles, defined as a group of neurons that fire together, are thought to underlie the neural representations of memories, perceptions, thoughts, motor programs, computations, or mental states (Lorente de No, 1938; Hebb, 1949; Cossart et al., 2003; Ikegaya et al., 2004; Sasaki et al., 2007; Buzsáki, 2010; Shepherd and Grillner, 2010; Yuste, 2015; Stringer et al., 2019b; Carillo-Reid and Yuste, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Ensembles have been found in mouse visual cortex during spontaneous activity and after visual stimulation.
source: Using two-photon calcium imaging, ensembles have been found in mouse visual cortex during spontaneous activity and after visual stimulation (Cossart et al., 2003; Miller et al., 2014; Carrillo-Reid et al., 2015b; Stringer et al., 2019c).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Optogenetic activation of ensembles can lead to behavioral effects consistent with the hypothesis that they represent perceptual or memory states.
source: The optogenetic activation of the ensembles can lead to behavioral effects consistent with the hypothesis that they represent perceptual or memory states (Carrillo-Reid et al., 2019; Marshel et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Single-cell tuning remains stable in visual cortex.
source: Interestingly, while single-cell tuning remains stable in visual cortex (Ranson, 2017; Jeon et al., 2018), a representational drift occurs across days (Deitch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: A representational drift occurs across days in visual cortex.
source: Interestingly, while single-cell tuning remains stable in visual cortex (Ranson, 2017; Jeon et al., 2018), a representational drift occurs across days (Deitch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Both stability and flexibility in different brain areas have been reported using single-cell recordings.
source: Both stability and flexibility in different brain areas have been reported using single-cell recordings (Lütcke et al., 2013; Ziv et al., 2013; Driscoll et al., 2017; Gonzalez et al., 2019; Rule and Harvey, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: There is a lack of multineuronal studies on cortical activity across days.
source: However, there is a lack of multineuronal studies on cortical activity across days.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: Longitudinal calcium imaging experiments were performed using two-photon multiplane microscopy in visual cortex of awake mice.
source: To study this, we performed longitudinal calcium imaging experiments using two-photon multiplane microscopy in visual cortex of awake mice and measured the responses of the same neurons for up to 46 days.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: Functional connectivity based on neuronal coactivity was used to detect neuronal ensembles.
source: Functional connectivity based on neuronal coactivity was used to detect neuronal ensembles.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the analysis approach.

claim: More than 50% of ensembles during spontaneous and visually evoked activity are stable.
source: We found that more than 50% of ensembles during spontaneous and visually evoked activity are stable.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3C.

claim: Transient ensembles appeared in only one session with no difference in the number of neurons or functional structure compared to stable ensembles.
source: The rest of the ensembles (transient ensembles) appeared in only one session with no difference in the number of neurons or functional structure compared to stable ensembles.
evidence: This is a finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: Approximately 68% of neurons in stable ensembles were preserved over weeks.
source: Analyzing stable ensembles, we found that ~68% of their neurons were preserved over weeks (stable neurons), whereas the rest were not (flexible neurons).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 4F.

claim: Stable neurons were more connected than neurons which were eventually lost.
source: Functional connectivity analysis revealed that stable neurons were more connected than neurons which were eventually lost.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the introduction and supported by data in Figure 4H.

claim: Two-photon calcium imaging was performed on pyramidal cells in layer 2/3 of the visual cortex from six transgenic mice.
source: We performed two-photon calcium imaging of pyramidal cells in layer 2/3 of the visual cortex from six transgenic mice (GCaMP6s, n = 4 animals; GCaMP6f, n = 2) through a cranial window to examine the stability of ensembles under visually evoked and spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental setup.

claim: Four mice expressed GCaMP6s and two mice expressed GCaMP6f.
source: We performed two-photon calcium imaging of pyramidal cells in layer 2/3 of the visual cortex from six transgenic mice (GCaMP6s, n = 4 animals; GCaMP6f, n = 2) through a cranial window to examine the stability of ensembles under visually evoked and spontaneous activity.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the experimental subjects.

claim: Mice were head-fixed in front of a blue screen monitor and free to run on a wheel.
source: We head-fixed mice in front of a blue screen monitor, and they were free to run on a wheel (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental setup, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Spontaneous neuronal activity was measured in response to a static blue screen.
source: We first measured the spontaneous neuronal activity in response to a static blue screen (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental protocol, with reference to Figure 1B.

claim: Visually evoked activity was recorded by displaying 50 times a single-orientation blue drifting gratings stimulus (2 s each) with a static blue screen between presentations (at 1–5 s random intervals).
source: Then, we recorded visually evoked activity by displaying 50 times a single-orientation blue drifting gratings stimulus (2 s each) with a static blue screen between presentations (at 1–5 s random intervals; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the visual stimulation protocol, with reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Three sessions were recorded each day for either spontaneous or evoked activity.
source: For either spontaneous or evoked activity, we recorded three sessions each day.
evidence: This is a methodological detail about the recording schedule.

claim: Multiplane calcium imaging was performed to track the same neurons across days.
source: To track the same neurons across days, multiplane calcium imaging was performed.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the imaging approach.

claim: A reference plane (0 µm) from day 1 was first located, then two extra planes 5 µm apart were recorded, above (–5 µm) and below (+ 5 µm) the reference plane.
source: A reference plane (0 µm) from day 1 was first located, then two extra planes 5 µm apart were recorded, above (–5 µm) and below (+ 5 µm) the reference plane (Figure 1D, left).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the multiplane imaging approach, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Maximum intensity projection frames were created from the three planes to assemble a single video per session.
source: After imaging, maximum intensity projection frames were created from the three planes to assemble a single video per session (Figure 1D, right).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the image processing approach, with reference to Figure 1D.

claim: Neurons with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) >18 dB were kept for analysis.
source: We then identified regions of interest (ROIs) of neuronal activity and kept neurons with peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) >18 dB (Figure 1E, left).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the quality control criteria, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: Calcium signals from each ROI were deconvolved for spike inference and thresholded to generate a binarized signal.
source: Calcium signals from each ROI were then deconvolved for spike inference and thresholded to generate a binarized signal, which we used to build spike raster plots (Figure 1E, right).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the signal processing approach, with reference to Figure 1E.

claim: The activity of the same neurons was recorded on days 2, 10, and 43 or 46.
source: We then analyzed all ROIs to build a binary raster plot (Figure 1F) and recorded the activity of the same neurons on days 2, 10, and 43 or 46 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the longitudinal recording schedule, with reference to Figures 1F and 1G.

claim: Some animals were imaged on day 43 and others on day 46, but data from those days were combined.
source: Some animals were imaged on day 43 and others on day 46, but we combined the data from those days (days 43–46; Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing how data from different time points were grouped.

claim: On day 1, an average of 83 ± 6 and 85 ± 5 (mean ± SEM) active neurons were found during spontaneous and evoked activity imaging periods, respectively.
source: On day 1, we found an average of 83 ± 6 and 85 ± 5 (mean ± SEM) active neurons during spontaneous and evoked activity imaging periods, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The number of active neurons was similar for days 1–10.
source: While the number of active neurons was similar for days 1–10, a significant decrease in the number of active neurons occurred in days 43–46, in both spontaneous and evoked activity (Figure 1H; 51 ± 10 neurons; p=0.023 and p=0.013, respectively).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1H and statistical significance values.

claim: A significant decrease in the number of active neurons occurred in days 43–46, in both spontaneous and evoked activity (51 ± 10 neurons; p=0.023 and p=0.013, respectively).
source: While the number of active neurons was similar for days 1–10, a significant decrease in the number of active neurons occurred in days 43–46, in both spontaneous and evoked activity (Figure 1H; 51 ± 10 neurons; p=0.023 and p=0.013, respectively).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1H and statistical significance values.

claim: Differences in z-displacement were similar across days (<4 µm).
source: Differences in z-displacement were similar across days (<4 µm, see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), but mice running speed tended to increase across days (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Mice running speed tended to increase across days.
source: Differences in z-displacement were similar across days (<4 µm, see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A), but mice running speed tended to increase across days (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The percentage of discarded neurons, with poor signal to noise (PSNR <18 dB), significantly increased from day 1 to days 43–46 (from 24 ± 1% to 37 ± 4%, mean ± SEM; p=0.034).
source: However, the percentage of discarded neurons, with poor signal to noise (PSNR <18 dB), significantly increased from day 1 to days 43–46 (from 24 ± 1% to 37 ± 4%, mean ± SEM; p=0.034; Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and statistical significance value.

claim: The loss of active cells on days 43–46 was likely due to a decrease in imaging quality.
source: Therefore, the loss of active cells on days 43–46 was likely due to a decrease in imaging quality, which could be partially explained by surgical attachment-related traumas (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The percentage of time that a neuron was active did not change over time and was ~15.5% either for spontaneous or evoked activity.
source: At the same time, the percentage of time that a neuron was active (the fraction of frames with activity) did not change over time and was ~15.5% either for spontaneous or evoked activity (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1I.

claim: Less than 50% of the neurons were repeatedly active across days, and this proportion became reduced over time.
source: Surprisingly, less than 50% of the neurons were repeatedly active across days, and this proportion became reduced over time (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1K.

claim: Even 5 min later, within day 1, only 42 ± 2% and 37 ± 4 % (mean ± SEM) of neurons remained active in the subsequent imaging session during spontaneous and evoked activity.
source: Even 5 min later, within day 1, only 42 ± 2% and 37 ± 4 % (mean ± SEM) of neurons remained active in the subsequent imaging session during spontaneous and evoked activity (gray in Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1K.

claim: The percentage of common neurons continued to decrease monotonically across days with significant decrements on days 10 and 43–46 in both spontaneous and evoked activity.
source: However, the percentage of common neurons continued to decrease monotonically across days with significant decrements on days 10 and 43–46 in both spontaneous and evoked activity (gray in Figure 1K).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1K.

claim: A significant number of neurons were still active 43–46 days later during spontaneous and evoked activity (17 ± 7 and 22 ± 8; mean ± SEM).
source: Despite the generalized decrease in the number of common neurons, we found a significant number of neuron which were still active 43–46 days later during spontaneous and evoked activity (17 ± 7 and 22 ± 8; mean ± SEM).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Common neurons had stable responses to locomotion correlation and tuning across days.
source: Moreover, these common neurons had stable responses to locomotion correlation and tuning across days (Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5) consistent with previous studies (Ranson, 2017; Jeon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplements 4 and 5, and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The neurons activated spontaneously or by visual stimulation are dynamically changing, and only a small proportion of neurons were repeatedly active across sessions from minutes to weeks.
source: We concluded that the neurons activated spontaneously or by visual stimulation are dynamically changing, and only a small proportion of neurons were repeatedly active across sessions from minutes to weeks.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis.

claim: An average of 4.57 ± 0.14 and 4.63 ± 0.14 (mean ± SEM) ensembles were identified on spontaneous and evoked activity sessions, with no significant differences between them.
source: Using this approach, we identified an average of 4.57 ± 0.14 and 4.63 ± 0.14 (mean ± SEM) ensembles on spontaneous and evoked activity sessions, with no significant differences between them (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: A stable ensemble is defined as the ensemble that maintains at least 50% of its neurons across days (Jaccard similarity ≥1/3).
source: We define a stable ensemble as the ensemble that maintains at least 50% of its neurons across days (Jaccard similarity ≥1/3; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a methodological definition used in the analysis.

claim: On day 1, stable ensembles constituted 54 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) of all ensembles during spontaneous activity, and 72 ± 4% (mean ± SEM) of ensembles during evoked activity.
source: On day 1, stable ensembles constituted 54 ± 3% (mean ± SEM) of all ensembles during spontaneous activity, and 72 ± 4% (mean ± SEM) of ensembles during evoked activity (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Stable ensembles were ~50% of all ensembles in both spontaneous or evoked activity on days 43–46.
source: Similar trends were observed on days 2 and 10, and stable ensembles were ~50% of all ensembles in both spontaneous or evoked activity on days 43–46 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3C.

claim: Visually evoked ensembles were more stable than spontaneous ones during the first days.
source: Visually evoked ensembles were more stable than spontaneous ones during the first days, but only some of them were similarly stable as spontaneous ones up to 43–46 days.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Some visually evoked ensembles could adapt to the stimulus.
source: This result suggests that some ensembles during evoked activity could adapt to the stimulus.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data.

claim: 0.8 ± 0.1 (mean ± SEM) stable ensembles were found in the shuffled activity compared with 2.8 ± 0.1 (mean ± SEM) stable ensembles from original data (p=1 × 10–66).
source: We found 0.8 ± 0.1 (mean ± SEM) stable ensembles in the shuffled activity compared with 2.8 ± 0.1 (mean ± SEM) stable ensembles from original data (p=1 × 10–66; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the control analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and statistical significance value.

claim: The total time of stable ensemble activation during a single session of spontaneous or evoked activity was significantly higher than in shuffled data (75.1 ± 2.7 s and 14.4 ± 1.3 s, respectively, mean ± SEM, p=2 × 10–57).
source: The total time of stable ensemble activation during a single session of spontaneous or evoked activity was significantly higher than in shuffled data (75.1 ± 2.7 s and 14.4 ± 1.3 s, respectively, mean ± SEM, p=2 × 10–57; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the control analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and statistical significance value.

claim: Stable ensembles could not be explained by chance.
source: In conclusion, stable ensembles could not be explained by chance, and they were not only reactivated during the following days but also their correlation with locomotion and tuning remained unchanged across days (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Stable ensembles' correlation with locomotion and tuning remained unchanged across days.
source: In conclusion, stable ensembles could not be explained by chance, and they were not only reactivated during the following days but also their correlation with locomotion and tuning remained unchanged across days (Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: Neuronal ensembles are true functional circuit elements and not an epiphenomenon of the population activity or a statistical artifact.
source: This speaks to the likelihood that neuronal ensembles are true functional circuit elements and not an epiphenomenon of the population activity or a statistical artifact.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the control analysis and data.

claim: Stable and transient ensembles have similar number of neurons.
source: We also investigated potential differences, other than stability, between stable and transient ensembles, finding similar number of neurons (Figure 3D) and network ensemble density (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3D.

claim: Stable and transient ensembles have similar network ensemble density.
source: We also investigated potential differences, other than stability, between stable and transient ensembles, finding similar number of neurons (Figure 3D) and network ensemble density (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3E.

claim: Ensemble robustness was significantly higher in stable than transient ensembles.
source: However, ensemble robustness, defined here as the product of ensemble duration and the similarity of its activity (see Materials and methods), was significantly higher in stable than transient ensembles (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3F.

claim: Stable ensembles are more robust than transient ones during spontaneous or evoked activity.
source: This result indicates that stable ensembles are more robust than transient ones during spontaneous or evoked activity (Figure 3—video 1 and Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3—video 1 and Figure 3—video 2.

claim: During spontaneous or evoked activity, approximately 50% of neurons belonged to only one stable ensemble ('single' neurons).
source: During spontaneous or evoked activity, approximately 50% of neurons belonged to only one stable ensemble ('single' neurons), while less than 20% of the neurons belonged to more than one ensemble ('shared' neurons), and the rest of the neurons were not part of any stable ensemble (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: Less than 20% of the neurons belonged to more than one ensemble ('shared' neurons).
source: During spontaneous or evoked activity, approximately 50% of neurons belonged to only one stable ensemble ('single' neurons), while less than 20% of the neurons belonged to more than one ensemble ('shared' neurons), and the rest of the neurons were not part of any stable ensemble (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: More than 60% of neurons of a stable ensemble observed on day 1 remained active on future sessions on days 1, 2, 10, and 43–46 during spontaneous and evoked activity ('stable' neurons).
source: More than 60% of neurons of a stable ensemble observed on day 1 remained active on future sessions on days 1, 2, 10, and 43–46 during spontaneous and evoked activity ('stable' neurons, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Less than 40% of neurons changed to another ensemble or stopped participating in detectable ensembles ('lost' neurons).
source: The rest of the neurons (<40%) changed to another ensemble or stopped participating in detectable ensembles ('lost' neurons).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: In subsequent sessions, 'new' neurons joined stable ensembles in a similar proportion as lost neurons.
source: Interestingly, in subsequent sessions, we found 'new' neurons joining stable ensembles in a similar proportion as lost neurons (lost and new neurons, Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: Functional connection density between stable neurons from the same ensemble (0.71 ± 0.01, mean ± SEM) was significantly higher than density from lost neurons during spontaneous or evoked activity (0.35 ± 0.02, mean ± SEM, p=7 × 10–55).
source: However, functional connection density between stable neurons from the same ensemble (0.71 ± 0.01, mean ± SEM) was significantly higher than density from lost neurons during spontaneous or evoked activity (0.35 ± 0.02, mean ± SEM, p=7 × 10–55, Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 4H and statistical significance value.

claim: Weak functional connectivity between lost neurons could explain why they are transient.
source: Therefore, weak functional connectivity between lost neurons could explain why they are transient, and high functional connectivity indicates possible lasting stability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis.

claim: High functional connectivity indicates possible lasting stability.
source: Therefore, weak functional connectivity between lost neurons could explain why they are transient, and high functional connectivity indicates possible lasting stability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data analysis.

claim: Single-neuron tuning is stable for up to 2 weeks.
source: Recent longitudinal studies have shown that single-neuron tuning is stable for up to 2 weeks (Ranson, 2017; Jeon et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Single-neuron selectivity is enhanced after learning.
source: Moreover, single-neuron selectivity is enhanced after learning (Poort et al., 2015; Henschke et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: No relevant differences in long-term stability were found between spontaneous and visually evoked activity.
source: Somewhat surprisingly, we did not find any relevant differences in long-term stability between spontaneous and visually evoked activity.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Ensembles during spontaneous activity were also active during visually evoked activity and vice versa.
source: Indeed, we found that ensembles during spontaneous activity were also active during visually evoked activity and vice versa (see 'S day 1 vs. E day n | E day 1 vs. S day n' in Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 5 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: More than 60% of neurons in spontaneous ensembles on day 1 were found to be tuned to a specific stimulus on the following weeks.
source: In fact, more than 60% of neurons in spontaneous ensembles on day 1 were found to be tuned to a specific stimulus on the following weeks.
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis.

claim: Sensory stimuli reactivate existing ensembles, which are already present in the spontaneous activity.
source: This result is consistent with the hypothesis that sensory stimuli reactivate existing ensembles, which are already present in the spontaneous activity (Miller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data, supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Cortical circuits maintain a basic homeostatic activity level, even in spite of perturbations.
source: Nevertheless, our method was sufficient to capture similar average activity from the neurons with sufficient levels of signal to noise over weeks (Figure 1I), agreeing with the hypothesis that cortical circuits maintain a basic homeostatic activity level, even in spite of perturbations (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007; Lütcke et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2013; Clopath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data, with reference to Figure 1I and supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Single-neuron responses were variable during the same repeated stimulation.
source: However, we found that single-neuron responses were variable during the same repeated stimulation (Montijn et al., 2016; Stringer et al., 2019a).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Transient silencing of neurons could be a neuronal correlate of the learning enhancement in deep neural networks.
source: This result is consistent with transient silencing of neurons (Prsa et al., 2017), which could be a neuronal correlate of the learning enhancement in deep neural networks (Srivastava et al., 2014; Rule and Harvey, 2019).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: 68% of neurons in stable ensembles continued to be active, while the rest of the neurons were replaced by new ones.
source: Stable ensembles were preserved across weeks and 68% of their neurons continued to be active, while the rest of the neurons were replaced by new ones (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is a finding from the data analysis, with reference to Figure 4F.

claim: The consistent number of neurons preserving their interactions within ensembles across weeks does not support a representational drift in cortical responses at the single neuronal level.
source: The consistent number of neurons preserving their interactions within ensembles across weeks does not support a representational drift in cortical responses at the single neuronal level (Driscoll et al., 2017, Rule and Harvey, 2019; Deitch et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data analysis, with citations to prior studies.

claim: One of the functions of ensembles could be to maintain a stable functional state in the midst of an ongoing homeostatic replacement of the activity of individual neuronal elements.
source: In fact, this could be precisely one of the functions of ensembles: to maintain a stable functional state in the midst of an ongoing homeostatic replacement of the activity of individual neuronal elements (Mrsic-Flogel et al., 2007; Lütcke et al., 2013; Hengen et al., 2013; Clopath et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The stability of ensembles could be based on the stability of dendritic spines.
source: The stability of ensembles could be based on the stability of dendritic spines (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2001).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data, supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: The weak connectivity of flexible neurons could be mediated by small spines, which appear and disappear over days.
source: The weak connectivity of flexible neurons could be mediated by small spines, which appear and disappear over days (Holtmaat et al., 2005), while the high connectivity of stable neurons could be maintained by large spines, which last for months (Holtmaat et al., 2005; Grutzendler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The high connectivity of stable neurons could be maintained by large spines, which last for months.
source: The weak connectivity of flexible neurons could be mediated by small spines, which appear and disappear over days (Holtmaat et al., 2005), while the high connectivity of stable neurons could be maintained by large spines, which last for months (Holtmaat et al., 2005; Grutzendler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed data, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The study did not image the activity of GABAergic interneurons.
source: One limitation of this study is that we did not image the activity of GABAergic interneurons, which are at least 28 different types based on the morphoelectric and transcriptomic classifications (Yuste et al., 2020; Gouwens et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a methodological limitation stated by the authors, with citations to prior work on interneuron classification.

claim: There are at least 28 different types of GABAergic interneurons based on morphoelectric and transcriptomic classifications.
source: One limitation of this study is that we did not image the activity of GABAergic interneurons, which are at least 28 different types based on the morphoelectric and transcriptomic classifications (Yuste et al., 2020; Gouwens et al., 2020; Yao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons could stabilize the cortical circuit.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons could stabilize the cortical circuit while somatostatin (SOM) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons could modulate the gain of pyramidal neurons (Bos et al., 2020; Millman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior knowledge, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Somatostatin (SOM) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons could modulate the gain of pyramidal neurons.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) interneurons could stabilize the cortical circuit while somatostatin (SOM) and vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons could modulate the gain of pyramidal neurons (Bos et al., 2020; Millman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior knowledge, supported by citations to prior work.

claim: PV interneurons in the visual cortex undergo faster homeostasis.
